title: Fatty Acid Synthesis: Building the Chain Two Carbons at a Time

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In fatty acid synthesis, what does each two-carbon addition after the first acetyl group cost, and where is each part paid?
cards.back: One malonyl CoA: one ATP at acetyl CoA carboxylase (to attach a carboxyl that later leaves as CO₂) and two NADPH on fatty acid synthase (to reduce the new C=O to CH₂).
cards.quote: every two carbons are added as one malonyl CoA, and each one has the same price

cards.front: Fatty acid synthesis happens mainly in the {{c1::cytoplasm}}, while beta-oxidation happens mainly in the mitochondrion.
cards.quote: Degradation happens mainly in the mitochondrion. Synthesis happens mainly in the cytoplasm.
cards.section: Why it is not beta-oxidation in reverse

cards.front: On what carrier does fatty acid synthesis hold its growing chain, and by what kind of arm?
cards.back: The acyl carrier protein (ACP), on a long phosphopantetheine arm that swings the chain between active sites. Beta-oxidation uses coenzyme A instead.
cards.quote: Synthesis carries them on a dedicated acyl carrier protein, ACP, using a long phosphopantetheine arm
cards.section: Why it is not beta-oxidation in reverse

cards.front: Beta-oxidation produces NADH and FADH2; fatty acid synthesis consumes {{c1::NADPH}}.
cards.quote: Degradation produces NADH and FADH2. Synthesis consumes NADPH.
cards.section: Why it is not beta-oxidation in reverse

cards.front: In the cytoplasm, in what redox states are the NAD and NADP pools kept, and why does that suit fat synthesis?
cards.back: NAD is kept mostly oxidized (NAD⁺), ready to accept electrons from burning fuel; NADP is kept mostly reduced (NADPH), ready to hand electrons to building.
cards.why: The extra phosphate on NADPH is a tag enzymes read, so the two pools do not mix on their own.
cards.quote: NADP is kept mostly reduced, as NADPH, ready to hand electrons to building.
cards.section: Why it is not beta-oxidation in reverse

cards.front: Why would a cell lose control if fatty acid synthesis were beta-oxidation run backward in the same compartment, on the same carrier and electron pool?
cards.back: It could not switch one direction on while holding the other off. New chains would sit beside the enzymes that burn them: a futile cycle that builds and tears down the same molecule and pays for both.
cards.quote: Separation lets the cell regulate each direction independently.
cards.section: Why it is not beta-oxidation in reverse

cards.front: Why must acetyl groups leave the mitochondrion as citrate for fat synthesis?
cards.back: Acetyl CoA cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Citrate (acetyl CoA joined to oxaloacetate) builds up when fuel is plentiful, is exported, and is cleaved back to acetyl CoA in the cytoplasm.
cards.quote: Acetyl CoA is made in the mitochondrion, but it cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.
cards.section: Stage 1: Transport. Citrate carries the acetyl group out

cards.front: A drug inhibits ATP-citrate lyase in hepatocytes while citrate export continues. Predict the effect on cytoplasmic acetyl CoA and on fatty acid synthesis.
cards.back: Cytoplasmic acetyl CoA falls and fatty acid synthesis tends to fall. Citrate still arrives but cannot be cleaved back into acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate, so the citrate route to ACC's substrate is cut.
cards.quote: There, ATP-citrate lyase spends an ATP to cleave it back into acetyl CoA and oxaloacetate.
cards.section: Stage 1: Transport. Citrate carries the acetyl group out

cards.front: Acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC) spends one ATP to attach a carboxyl group, supplied as bicarbonate, to acetyl CoA, making {{c1::malonyl CoA}}.
cards.quote: In the cytoplasm, acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC) spends one ATP to attach a carboxyl group, supplied as bicarbonate, to acetyl CoA.

cards.front: What cofactor does acetyl CoA carboxylase carry, and how is it attached to the enzyme?
cards.back: Biotin, a vitamin tethered to a lysine. It acts as a swinging arm that carries the carboxyl group from one active site to another.
cards.quote: ACC carries biotin, a vitamin tethered to a lysine.

cards.front: Why is ACC1, rather than a later enzyme, the committed step of fatty acid synthesis?
cards.back: Its product, malonyl CoA, has essentially one fate: addition to a fatty acid. ACC1 is the first step that serves fat synthesis and nothing else, so the cell's fast controls act there.
cards.quote: So ACC1 is the first step that serves fat synthesis and nothing else

cards.front: Rats eat a diet rich in raw egg white, which contains avidin. Predict the effect on malonyl CoA production and on pyruvate carboxylase.
cards.back: Both fall. Avidin binds biotin so tightly that it sequesters the vitamin, and both ACC and pyruvate carboxylase depend on a biotin arm to carry the carboxyl group.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's rule that ACC uses the same biotin CO₂-taxi trick as pyruvate carboxylase.
cards.quote: The culprit was avidin, an egg-white protein that binds biotin so tightly

cards.front: The four repeating steps on fatty acid synthase are Condensation, Reduction, Dehydration, Reduction, abbreviated {{c1::CRDR}}.
cards.quote: The job names spell the cycle: Condensation, Reduction, Dehydration, Reduction, or CRDR.
cards.section: Stage 3: Elongation, one turn at a time

cards.front: During condensation on fatty acid synthase, what happens to the malonyl unit, and what product forms in turn one?
cards.back: The malonyl unit loses its extra carboxyl as CO₂, and the carbon next to it attacks the primer's C=O, giving the four-carbon acetoacetyl-ACP.
cards.quote: The malonyl unit loses its extra carboxyl as CO₂, and the carbon that was next to it attacks the primer's C=O.

cards.front: A liver extract makes palmitate from carbon-14 bicarbonate in one run and from uniformly carbon-14 acetyl CoA in another. How does the palmitate label compare, and what does it show?
cards.back: Bicarbonate run: little to none in palmitate; acetyl CoA run: labeled chain. The carbon ACC adds leaves as CO₂ at condensation in every turn, so it is a leaving group, not a building block.
cards.quote: the classic proof that the CO₂ is a leaving group, not a building block.

cards.front: Why does the cell spend an ATP to attach a carboxyl group that leaves as CO₂ one step later?
cards.back: Joining two acetyl groups directly is uphill and easily undone. Losing CO₂ is strongly downhill, and coupling that loss to the new C–C bond makes each join effectively one-way.
cards.quote: Losing CO₂ is strongly downhill, and coupling that loss to the new carbon–carbon bond makes each join effectively one-way.

cards.front: After condensation on fatty acid synthase, name the three steps that turn the β-keto group into CH₂, in order, with the domain for each.
cards.back: Reduction by ketoreductase (KR, NADPH) to an alcohol; dehydration by dehydratase (DH) to a C=C; reduction by enoyl reductase (ER, NADPH) to saturated CH₂.
cards.quote: Each NADPH delivers two, as a hydride, so it takes two NADPH, added in two steps with a dehydration between them.

cards.front: Why does reducing the β-carbon's C=O all the way to CH₂ take exactly two NADPH?
cards.back: The carbon's oxidation state falls from +2 to −2, which takes four electrons, and each NADPH delivers two, as a hydride.
cards.quote: That takes four electrons (the carbon's oxidation state falls from +2 to −2).

cards.front: In a palmitate made by fatty acid synthase, where do the primer's two carbons end up, and why?
cards.back: At the far, methyl end. Each turn adds two carbons at the end nearest the sulfur (the thioester), so the primer is pushed outward.
cards.quote: so the primer's two carbons end up at the far, methyl end of the finished fatty acid.

cards.front: A fatty acid synthase has a ketoreductase domain that cannot use NADPH; all other domains work. Predict what accumulates and whether chains lengthen.
cards.back: The β-ketoacyl-ACP from the first condensation (acetoacetyl-ACP) accumulates, and chains do not lengthen. Without the first reduction, dehydration and the second reduction cannot follow, so no saturated butyryl-ACP forms for the next turn.
cards.why: Rests on the CRDR order: the next three steps exist to turn the new C=O into CH₂ before the chain returns to KS.
cards.quote: A fatty acid's chain is all CH₂, so the other three steps share one job: turn that C=O into CH₂.

cards.front: Using the per-turn price, compute the acetyl CoA, ATP and NADPH needed for one palmitate (C16) built from cytoplasmic acetyl CoA.
cards.back: Turns = (16 − 2)/2 = 7. ATP = 7 (one per malonyl CoA at ACC). NADPH = 2 × 7 = 14. Acetyl CoA = 7 + 1 = 8.
cards.why: Charging 8 ATP is the common error: the primer is used as acetyl CoA and never goes through ACC.
cards.quote: Seven turns: 8 acetyl CoA, 7 ATP, 14 NADPH.

cards.front: At what chain length does fatty acid synthase usually stop, and in what form does it release the chain?
cards.back: Sixteen carbons; thioesterase releases free palmitate.
cards.quote: FAS stops at 16 and releases free palmitate.

cards.front: Compute the acetyl CoA, ATP and NADPH for one stearate (C18) from cytoplasmic acetyl CoA. FAS releases palmitate, which is reactivated to palmitoyl CoA (1 ATP) before an ER elongase adds two carbons.
cards.back: Turns = (18 − 2)/2 = 8. ATP = 8 at ACC + 1 to reactivate palmitate = 9. NADPH = 2 × 8 = 16. Acetyl CoA = 8 + 1 = 9.
cards.quote: an elongase on the endoplasmic reticulum adds the last two carbons at the same per-turn price.

cards.front: Extend the per-turn rule to arachidate (C20, saturated) made from cytoplasmic acetyl CoA, with palmitate reactivated once and then elongated twice on the ER (two elongase rounds, each at the same per-turn price). Compute acetyl CoA, ATP and NADPH.
cards.back: Turns = (20 − 2)/2 = 9. ATP = 9 at ACC + 1 reactivation = 10. NADPH = 2 × 9 = 18. Acetyl CoA = 9 + 1 = 10.
cards.why: Rests on elongases using malonyl CoA at the same per-turn price as FAS, as in the stearate example.
cards.quote: Elongases extend the chain from malonyl CoA at the same per-turn price, as in the stearate example.

cards.front: In the palmitate ledger, why do 7 HCO₃⁻ go in and 7 CO₂ come out?
cards.back: Seven bicarbonates are fixed at ACC to make the seven malonyl CoA, and each of those carboxyls leaves as CO₂ at condensation.
cards.quote: Seven bicarbonates go in at ACC and seven CO₂ come out at condensation.

cards.front: Seven CRDR turns build palmitate. Why does the balanced ledger release 6 H₂O rather than 7?
cards.back: Seven dehydrations release 7 H₂O; thioesterase uses 1 to cut palmitate free from ACP. 7 − 1 = 6.
cards.quote: Seven dehydrations release seven waters, and the thioesterase uses one to cut palmitate free, leaving six.

cards.front: How does the citrate shuttle turn cytoplasmic NADH into NADPH, and what does each pass cost?
cards.back: Oxaloacetate is reduced to malate (spending NADH); malic enzyme decarboxylates malate to pyruvate, making NADPH; in the mitochondrion pyruvate carboxylase remakes oxaloacetate for one ATP.
cards.quote: In effect the shuttle turns an NADH into an NADPH for the price of an ATP.
cards.section: Paying the bill: NADPH and delivery

cards.front: Per palmitate, the citrate shuttle via malic enzyme can supply up to {{c1::8}} of the 14 NADPH; the pentose phosphate pathway and other routes supply the rest.
cards.back: The shuttle runs once per acetyl group delivered.
cards.quote: It runs once per acetyl group delivered, so it can supply up to 8 of the 14 NADPH.
cards.section: Paying the bill: NADPH and delivery

cards.front: Count the total ATP per palmitate, delivery included, when every oxaloacetate returns to the mitochondrion as pyruvate via malic enzyme. How many NADPH remain for the pentose phosphate pathway?
cards.back: ATP-citrate lyase 8 + pyruvate carboxylase 8 + ACC 7 = 23 ATP. The shuttle gives 8 NADPH (for 8 NADH), leaving 14 − 8 = 6.
cards.quote: delivering 8 acetyl groups as citrate costs 8 more at ATP-citrate lyase
cards.section: Paying the bill: NADPH and delivery

cards.front: Suppose that for one palmitate, 4 of the 8 oxaloacetates return via malic enzyme and 4 return as malate. Compute total ATP and the NADPH that must come from other routes.
cards.back: ATP = 8 (ATP-citrate lyase) + 4 (pyruvate carboxylase) + 7 (ACC) = 19. Shuttle NADPH = 4, so 14 − 4 = 10 from the pentose phosphate pathway and other routes.
cards.why: Interpolates the lesson's two routes: each malic-enzyme pass yields one NADPH and costs one ATP at pyruvate carboxylase; the malate route costs neither.
cards.quote: The pentose phosphate pathway and other routes supply the rest, and the real split varies by tissue.
cards.section: Paying the bill: NADPH and delivery

cards.front: Hepatocytes lack cytoplasmic malic enzyme but export citrate normally, so every oxaloacetate returns as malate. Predict the ATP bill per palmitate and where all the NADPH must come from.
cards.back: The ATP bill falls to 15 (8 at ATP-citrate lyase + 7 at ACC, none at pyruvate carboxylase), but the shuttle makes no NADPH, so all 14 must come from the pentose phosphate pathway and other routes.
cards.why: Rests on the delivery table: the malate return route spends no ATP and makes no NADPH.
cards.quote: the rest depends on where the oxaloacetate goes
cards.section: Paying the bill: NADPH and delivery

cards.front: Which enzyme phosphorylates ACC, and what does phosphorylation do? Which enzyme reverses it?
cards.back: AMPK, the cell's low-fuel sensor, phosphorylates ACC and turns it off; PP2A removes the phosphate and turns it on.
cards.quote: AMPK, the cell's low-fuel sensor, phosphorylates ACC

cards.front: How do citrate and palmitoyl CoA allosterically control acetyl CoA carboxylase?
cards.back: Citrate (abundant fuel) makes ACC polymerize into active filaments; palmitoyl CoA, the end product, depolymerizes them, a feedback brake.
cards.quote: citrate (abundant fuel) makes ACC polymerize into active filaments

cards.front: In a well-fed liver, mitochondrial citrate builds up. Predict two separate ways this pushes fatty acid synthesis forward.
cards.back: Exported citrate delivers acetyl groups to the cytoplasm (cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase), and citrate allosterically activates ACC by driving it into active filaments, so more malonyl CoA is made.
cards.quote: when fuel is plentiful, citrate builds up and is exported to the cytoplasm.
cards.section: Stage 1: Transport. Citrate carries the acetyl group out

cards.front: Which hormones turn ACC on and off, and how do insulin and glucose act on fat synthesis over hours to days?
cards.back: Insulin turns ACC on; glucagon and epinephrine turn it off. Over hours to days, insulin and glucose switch on the ACC and FAS genes via SREBP-1c and ChREBP.
cards.quote: Over hours to days, insulin and glucose also switch on the ACC and FAS genes, through the transcription factors SREBP-1c and ChREBP.

cards.front: What is malonyl CoA's second job, and which form of ACC makes much of the malonyl CoA that does it?
cards.back: It blocks CPT-I, the gate long-chain fat must pass to be burned in the mitochondrion. Much of that pool comes from ACC2 on the mitochondrion; ACC1 mostly feeds synthesis.
cards.quote: Much of the malonyl CoA that does this blocking is made by a second form of the enzyme, ACC2, which sits on the mitochondrion

cards.front: Epinephrine reaches the liver during a long run. Predict the effects on ACC, malonyl CoA, CPT-I and fatty acid oxidation.
cards.back: ACC is turned off, malonyl CoA falls, synthesis slows for lack of its building block, and the block on CPT-I lifts, so fat enters the mitochondrion and oxidation rises.
cards.why: Epinephrine is an off signal for ACC, like glucagon; exercise also switches AMPK on.
cards.quote: Synthesis slows for lack of its building block, and the block on CPT-I lifts, so fat enters the mitochondrion and is burned.

cards.front: A mouse carries an ACC mutant that AMPK cannot phosphorylate. During exercise, predict malonyl CoA levels and fat oxidation compared with a normal mouse.
cards.back: Malonyl CoA stays higher and fat oxidation rises less. Exercise activates AMPK, but AMPK cannot switch the mutant ACC off, so CPT-I is not relieved.
cards.quote: Exercise switches AMPK on, and so, in experiments, may the diabetes drug metformin

cards.front: Ethanol metabolism floods the liver with NADH, turns AMPK down and turns fat-making genes up. Why is beta-oxidation suppressed by two separate routes?
cards.back: ACC runs harder, malonyl CoA rises and CPT-I closes, so fat cannot enter the mitochondrion; and the high NADH-to-NAD⁺ ratio slows beta-oxidation directly. Less burning plus more building gives fatty liver.
cards.quote: Beta-oxidation is hit twice: the gate is shut, and the high NADH-to-NAD⁺ ratio slows beta-oxidation directly.

cards.front: A drug selectively blocks ACC2 while ACC1 keeps working. Predict how fat oxidation and fat synthesis respond, and why the usual see-saw is partly broken.
cards.back: Synthesis can continue on ACC1's malonyl CoA, but the mitochondrial pool that blocks CPT-I falls, so oxidation would tend to rise. Building and burning are no longer strictly reciprocal.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's split: ACC2 makes much of the CPT-I-blocking malonyl CoA, while ACC1 mostly feeds synthesis.
cards.quote: So when the cell is building fat, it also tends to close the door on oxidation.

cards.front: In one proposed mechanism, metformin inhibits mitochondrial Complex I. Trace the effect from the AMP:ATP ratio to fatty acid oxidation, and state the caveat.
cards.back: AMP:ATP rises, AMPK switches on and phosphorylates ACC, malonyl CoA falls, synthesis slows and CPT-I opens, so oxidation rises. Caveat: how metformin lowers blood sugar is debated, and much of it does not need AMPK.
cards.quote: Malonyl CoA falls, so synthesis slows and CPT-I opens, and oxidation rises.

cards.front: Why are linoleate and alpha-linolenate essential fatty acids for mammals?
cards.back: Mammalian desaturases can place double bonds only out to carbon 9 from the carboxyl end. The omega-6 and omega-3 positions (carbons 12 and 15 in an 18-carbon chain) lie beyond, so these fats must be eaten.
cards.quote: mammalian desaturases can place a double bond as far out as carbon 9, and no farther.

cards.front: Why does the antiplatelet effect of a single aspirin dose fade only gradually, over about a week?
cards.back: Aspirin permanently acetylates cyclooxygenase. Platelets have no nucleus, so they make little or no replacement enzyme; the effect fades as new platelets replace the old.
cards.quote: Platelets have no nucleus, so they make little or no replacement enzyme.

cards.front: Which stereoisomer of the 3-hydroxyacyl intermediate does fatty acid synthesis make, and which does mitochondrial beta-oxidation use?
cards.back: Synthesis (at ketoreductase) makes the D-isomer; beta-oxidation runs through the L-isomer.
cards.quote: the first reduction (KR) makes D-3-hydroxyacyl intermediates, while mitochondrial beta-oxidation runs through the L-isomers.
cards.section: One more tell: D and L

cards.front: Odd-chain fatty acids start from a three-carbon primer, {{c1::propionyl CoA}}, instead of acetyl CoA.
cards.quote: Odd-chain fatty acids start from a three-carbon primer, propionyl CoA, instead of acetyl CoA.
